Jensen just laid out where the ASIC industry might be headed.

The pattern: ASIC contractors thrive right up until the customer gets big enough to take the tooling in-house. Early on, you pay an ASIC house a fat turnkey margin because you lack the engineering muscle to do it yourself. Once your volume is massive and your team is deep, that margin becomes money you're giving away.

That end-state has a name: Customer Owned Tooling. The customer keeps ownership of the design, RTL through GDSII and the masks, and works directly with TSMC. They pay for foundry, IP, and packaging, but they stop paying an ASIC partner a turnkey cut on top. Apple is the textbook case. At iPhone scale, Apple would never hand 50 to 60% gross margin to a contractor for its A-series and M-series. So it doesn't.

Jensen's prediction is simply that AI accelerators follow the same road. If TPUs, Trainium, or MTIA grow into a truly large business, the natural destination is COT, not perpetual fat margins for a Broadcom-style partner. When a single hyperscaler's accelerator program reaches Apple-phone scale, the economics have to shift.

If the AI accelerator market for a single hyperscaler becomes Apple-phone-sized, the value capture shifts: Foundry + HBM + advanced packaging stay expensive either way.

The fat “ASIC services” margin gets compressed.
The customer (Google, Amazon, etc.) keeps more of the silicon economics and more control over the roadmap.

Nvidia’s counter is that programmability, software, interconnect, and the rate of architectural improvement still justify paying for a merchant GPU even at high margins and that many “ASICs” will not actually beat that package.

What happened to DeepSeek V1, V2, V3, and V4.0?  

Gone. Forgotten.

When do you still pay up for Astra or Fable 5.1 over a cheap coder like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash?

Hard reasoning. Novel problems. Multi hour computer use. Low error tolerance. Vendor tools and safety.

Compression is not free. A smaller cache is a lossier memory. It shows up on long horizon jobs, big codebases, deep context. Not on short benches.

Long horizon agent loops that run for hours. The further back a constraint or instruction sits, the softer its recall. It can drop a rule you set 100K tokens ago and not flag that it did.

Large codebases. Multi file work where a change in file A has to stay consistent with a contract defined in file F. Subtle cross file references and long range dependencies are exactly what a compressed cache blurs.

Multi hop reasoning over long documents. Chains where step 7 depends on a detail from step 2, buried deep in context. The intermediate state is where fidelity leaks.

None of these show up on short, well scoped coding and terminal benches, which is why it looks level with last gen frontier there.
